# 09-karsa — sources

Back-test entry `09-karsa.yaml`: Karsa, buying and saving dollar stablecoins where the local currency inflates
(YC Winter 2025). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim from the page named; "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent.

Main sources:
- [HN] Launch HN: Karsa (YC W25), 2025-01-30, 215 comments — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42879661 (a comment is cited by its own item URL)
- [LYC] Launch YC: Karsa, the global dollar account — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MgV-karsa-the-global-dollar-account
- [YCP] YC company page — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/karsa (now "a stablecoin neobank")
- [DAWN23] Dawn, on digital currencies in Pakistan as "a high-tech replacement for hawala-hundi" (headline shortened here), 2023-10-30 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1784968
- [AAJ] Aaj News, "Dollars disappear from open market due to hoarding", 2022-12-15 — https://english.aaj.tv/news/30306930
- [DAWN21] Dawn, "Biometric proof must for buying $500 or above: SBP", 2021-10 — https://www.dawn.com/news/1650577/biometric-proof-must-for-buying-500-or-above-sbp
- [NAYA] NayaPay help, the SBP's annual card limit — https://help.nayapay.com/article/242-what-is-the-annual-card-based-international-transactions-limit-set-by-the-sbp
- [ARAB] Arab News, "Pakistan says has no plans to freeze foreign currency accounts", 2023-06-12 — https://www.arabnews.pk/pakistan/pakistan-says-has-no-plans-to-freeze-foreign-currency-accounts-2320266

## Market

The public material supports **Pakistan** best: the founder's family ([HN] "his uncle in Pakistan"; [LYC] "Shahryar's
family in Pakistan still acutely faces this problem"), the first live sellers ([YCP] "Pakistan, India, Nigeria,
Kenya, Paraguay"), the PKR page discussed in the thread, and the most press on the problem. The segment and all twenty
respondents are in Pakistan. The eval's loader (`instructions/corpus.py`, `MARKET_CURRENCY`) knows only GB, US, IE, FR,
DE, IN, CA and AU, so per the brief the `market` line is **US** (`language: en-US`) and every money value is in USD.
Dollars are also the unit these savers think and buy in (the fee is 1% of the dollars bought). keel-cloud's own
`Market` table does not know PK either, though `Market.chosen` would take PK with an explicit currency.

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** People in Pakistan who earn in rupees and save.
   [HN] "when Shahryar tried explaining [it] to his uncle in Pakistan, it was all jargon until he explained
   stablecoins, which immediately clicked." → `roles[saver]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Keep savings from losing value.
   [HN] "buy and save in stablecoins to protect against currency instability and inflation"; "Over a billion people
   live in countries with severe inflation and are unable to protect their wealth due to strict capital controls."
   → `context.job`, `statements.problem`.

3. **When / where.** When they have rupees left over and want dollars, with the bank and the exchange companies in the
   way. [HN] "earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year"; "good luck getting a foreign currency
   account." [AAJ] dollars "not being readily available in the open market". [DAWN21] exchange companies must "conduct
   biometric verification for all foreign currency sale transactions equivalent to $500 and above". [NAYA] card-based
   international transactions "of up to USD 30,000 per year", "per individual, not per card".
   → `context.circumstance`. Author's choice: the occasion "payday", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out
   of 3, and Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most"): no public figure says how often.

4. **Which people (the comparable group).** [HN] "(1) earning in a currency thatʼs inflating 20-30% year-over-year, (2)
   whoʼs structurally limited from dollar access, and (3) makes payments abroad regularly". → `context.segment`
   (narrowed to Pakistan, the market chosen; condition 3 becomes the Importance rival "Paying for things abroad").

5. **Who pays.** The saver, alone. [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee". → `persona.decision_maker:
   same_person`, Buyer and payer "Nobody else". Author's choice: no other role is named.

6. **Mechanism.** [HN] "Karsa looks and feels like a bank/currency exchange to an average user—they choose an amount
   and buy dollar-denominated stablecoins at a market price. But under the hood, we route our supply from a network of
   verified peer-to-peer stablecoin traders"; "A seller sets their price and deposits money in an escrow smart
   contract"; the buyer "has to send a fiat payment (e.g., bank transfer, payment app, etc.) to the sellerʼs local
   account + upload a photo for verification"; "we ... release the escrowed stablecoins to a digital wallet weʼve
   created for the buyer." → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`, the Compatibility and Adoption friction items
   (the ID card and payment photo item comes from the same step and from [HN] "we do KYC"). Commitment's step "buy a
   small first amount of dollars" is the author's.

7. **Price.** [HN] "We currently take a 1% transaction fee, though we eventually intend to adjust it proportionally to
   regional FX rates." → `commercial.price` {1, 3, month}: author's arithmetic, 1% of about $100 to $300 of dollars
   bought a month (the amount is the author's choice). Existing sacrifice {5, 15, month}: the premium paid today,
   from [DAWN23] (the PKR-to-USDT premium over the official rate reportedly widened from Rs5-6 to Rs8-9) and [HN] (India:
   "the bid-ask spreads are calamitous - to the tune of 5-6% per side" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42885086),
   taken as 3% to 5% of the same $100 to $300 (author's arithmetic). Ability to pay is derived by code (7% to 60%).

8. **Occasions.** [HN] "Users in these countries already use exchanges like Binance almost like a dollar checking
   account" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42880301 ; a user in Bolivia: "there’s a limit of 50 USD on USD
   transactions per week for each bank" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42881375 (outside the chosen market, so
   it shaped the statement, not a respondent); [DAWN23] "A need for wealth preservation in the face of high inflation and
   currency devaluation"; "a high share of activity happening in Pakistan is through peer-to-peer exchanges".

No respondent carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Open
- Market: the loader knows no PK currency, so the entry is US / en-US with dollars while the segment and every
  respondent are in Pakistan. A Keel study in Pakistan would ask in English or Urdu and might price in rupees; that is
  not tested here.
- The verdict was scripted to be plausible and not obviously "build": the problem holds (most had it, most say getting
  savings into dollars is one of their two, today's ways fall short); the solution splits on paying a seller they have
  never met (eight of thirteen would); the commercial side splits on what the problem costs them today (several pay
  little or nothing besides inflation) and on taking a first step, while the 1% fee itself holds. This is the author's
  reading of the thread's sceptics, not a measured result.
- Two respondents transpose accounts from India (the KYC wall, the spread) to Pakistan; the Bolivian $50-a-week limit
  shaped the founder's statement only.
- Existing sacrifice picks use `period: quarter` (the corpus's convention), although the registry's recall period for a
  monthly cost reads "last month"; the values are three months' worth.
- DAWN23's headline is shortened in the source list: its first word holds a string banned from these files.
- The amount bought a month ($100 to $300), the occasion "payday", the window and the Prevalence bin are the author's.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: No groups were made and that is right, because a lost payment to a seller, a father who won't trust sending money to a stranger, and bills against a flat salary are three different stories with no common group they belong in.
whys.g2: There is no junk, explicit or off-topic answer on the line that got grouped, since no groups exist and all three answers are real replies from people in this situation.

founder.order_why: The flow runs sensibly from context to problem, idea, payment and interviews, but 'who has to agree before they can buy' (14) comes after cost and price (12-13) when it belongs straight after 'who decides' (10-11).
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14 (with 15-16 following from 14): for a saver who decides alone, 'would someone else decide?' and 'who else has to agree?' are nearly the same question. Screens 17 and 19 also overlap, as both ask what first step to offer: the first real step and a pilot.
founder.missing: No screen visibly asks what language and currency to run the study in: my savers are in Pakistan and may answer in Urdu and think in rupees, so 'where you sell' alone doesn't settle that. No screen by its title asks about trust either, and my biggest risk is whether they will send money to a seller they have never met and hand over ID, though the idea cards may touch on this.

PRIMARY.order_why: The flow from screening to the idea to the questions is sensible, but the question about how much value I lost last month comes after the idea card when it would feel more natural to talk about my own situation before being shown Karsa.
PRIMARY.missing: How I actually get dollars today, such as Binance or the open market, including the chats with sellers for each trade, the premium I pay, and whether I can trust the seller.

screens.why1: Choosing who asks my savers belongs here, just before the study goes out, and it does not repeat anything I have already answered.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how savers answer, the last step before sending is obviously who receives the link.

screens.why_b1: The headline says "People disagree" and gives Price's 4 of 7, but the page says the verdict is the worst card and Commitment "Did not hold", so the deciding result isn't the one beside the verdict, and Price and Commitment get different words for the same 4 of 7 against a bar of 5.
screens.why_b2: This page has no chart, but most count lines show who is counted, over how many and the bar at a glance; I need a second look at Ability to pay, which counts people naming my price rather than comparing the fee with what they lose today, and at the jump from card 4 to card 6.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment carry the dimension names and the exact lines I checked: "The saver decides, and nobody else has to agree" and "Most savers would buy a small first amount of dollars now."
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what this means for Karsa or what to do next; the sentence under the verdict explains how the interview was built, and the cards only report status.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and nothing is claimed beyond the 7 who answered, but "bigger than you thought: they lose more today than you estimated" is a soft overstatement on 4 of 6 sitting exactly at the bar, and the page never says 7 is a small group.
screens.instead: Did not hold: only 4 of these 7 would buy a small first amount now, 1 short of the 5 you needed, and the 1% fee fell short by the same margin, while 6 of 7 decide alone; read why the 3 said no before you change the fee, and remember this is only 7 people.

screens.why_b1: The verdict says the belief is holding and bigger than I thought, and 4 of 6 against a bar of 4 of 6 sits right beside it, though 'bigger' is not what that number shows.
screens.why_b2: The count over 6 people and the 2-in-3 bar are plain, but it takes a second look to separate my 1.5% from the 4-of-6 bar and to see how a 0-to-10 scale and a strip of cells fit together.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the belief as my saver's loss, but 'Existing sacrifice' is not my word, and 'the rupees they move to dollars' and 'the value of the rupees they are saving up' are two different bases for the percentage.
screens.why_b4: The So line confirms the cost exists and points me to the Price card, which I have already read, so 'next' is wrong and it never says what this means for the idea or for my 1% fee.
screens.why_b5: The screen shows n and says 'a lean, not a call', but 'bigger than you thought: they lose more today than you estimated' overstates a result that only just reaches the bar, with two of six below 1.5%, one exactly on it and the highest figure a lone 9%.
screens.instead: Holding, just: 4 of 6 lose 1.5% or more, exactly at your bar, and 2 lose less (answers run from 0.3% to 9%); it's a small group, so it's a lean, and a loss around 1.5% leaves little room above your 1% fee, so test the fee against it before you raise it.

screens.why_b1: "People disagree" sits directly above "4 of 7 at 1% or more · bar 5 of 7 · 1 short", so I can see that my price missed the bar and by how much.
screens.why_b2: The bands show what percentage people think is fair, the for and against marks and the strip show 4 for and 3 against out of 7, and the marker sits plainly at 5.
screens.why_b3: It is recognisably my 1% fee, but I charge 1% per purchase of dollars, and "1% of the rupees they move to dollars a month" is clumsier than how I would say it.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and sends me to the Insights tab, without saying whether to keep 1%, change it, or treat the two refusals as a different problem from price.
screens.why_b5: The small group is flagged as "a lean, not a call" and n stays visible, but the So line turns an answer about what fee feels fair into "would pay your price", which is a soft overstatement.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 call 1% or more fair, 1 short of the bar, but only one of the other 3 wants a lower fee and the 2 who refuse have reasons other than the size of the fee, so keep 1% for now and look at trust and need before cutting it; it's a small group, so this is only a lean.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits directly above "4 of 7 named your price or more · 5 needed", so I know this has no answer yet and which number decides that.
screens.why_b2: I can see four people counted and a bar of 3 of 4, but it takes a second look to work out why the axis stops at 3, what the fifth, ghost cell is, and how this bar relates to the 5 needed.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly beside 6 of 7 decided alone against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know my belief held and which number decides it.

screens.why_b2: At first look I can see that it counts answers to whether they would buy, over 7 people (4 for, 1 probably not, 2 no), with the bar marked at 5 of 7.

screens.why_b1: Both boxes state the verdict (People disagree, Did not hold) directly above the deciding number and the bar: 4 of 7, bar 5 of 7, 1 short.
screens.why_b3: The names are the lines I checked and the Commitment belief is word for word mine; the Price belief is in my terms, a 1% fee on what they move to dollars, even if I charge it per transaction rather than by the month.
screens.why_b4: Neither box says what the result means for Karsa, and the Commitment box leaves its question with no answers and no next step, so I have to work out for myself that I should fix trust in the seller step before touching the fee.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and the count line honestly explains why Commitment has no quotes, but no line says that 7 people is few, and a flat "Did not hold" on one person short reads firmer than 7 answers can carry.
screens.why_b6: I typed a fee belief and the quotes show the objection is often not the 1%: a seller who never released and took Farhan's money, Usman's father vetoing a transfer to a stranger, and Nadia, who already has a dollar account and worries about bills, which also questions my segment.
screens.instead: Say at the top: "7 people, so read this as a signal: of the 3 against the 1% fee, 2 raised something other than price (a lost payment, a father who won't trust a stranger) and 1 already has a dollar account, so show how escrow protects the buyer before you change the fee; nobody was asked why on Commitment, because 2 of the 3 against never saw that question and the third was asked on Price."

screens.why1: As the first screen of a study about saving in dollars from rupees, it makes sense to check straight away whether I have a foreign currency account.
screens.why2: The words foreign currency account are familiar to me from the banks here, but the negative in 'do you have no' makes me stop and read it twice.
screens.why3: I know for certain whether I hold a foreign currency account, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover everything, but against a negative question 'Yes' could mean I have no account or that I do have one, so the two options blur.
screens.why5: Nothing of any product leaks to me and it still means the founder's 'no foreign currency account', but the segment wording has been pasted into a question and reads stiffly.
screens.why6: It is short and one question, but heard once the negative is easy to miss, and with no options read out a 'yes' or 'no' from me could be taken either way.
screens.instead: Do you have a foreign currency account at a bank? Yes; No

screens.why1: After being asked about not having a foreign currency account, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: I have used Binance P2P so stablecoin, wallet and escrow are words I know, but 'with no jargon' is itself an odd word for me and 'verified local seller' leaves me wondering who verified them.
screens.why3: Having leftover rupees, paying a seller by bank transfer or mobile wallet and getting dollars back is exactly what I already do when I save.
screens.why4: The screen is a card to read, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: 'Looks like a currency exchange, with no jargon' sounds like the company's design brief rather than something told to me, and the belief line only repeats the first line, though the idea itself is clear and meant to be shown.
screens.why6: The short sentences say well and there are no symbols, but it is seven sentences to hold in one hearing, and the last one repeats 'dollar stablecoins in a wallet in your name' almost word for word from before.
screens.instead: Imagine Karsa, an app for turning your rupees into dollar stablecoins. You choose an amount and pay a verified local seller by bank transfer or mobile wallet; the app holds the seller's stablecoins in escrow, then releases them to a wallet in your name. The people building it believe this would make saving in dollars simpler than arranging each deal in chat.

screens.why1: Right after the idea and under 'What you do today', it makes sense to ask what my current way of saving is costing me.
screens.why2: 'How much of the value of the rupees you were saving did you miss' is confusing, because I would talk about the premium I paid over the rate or what the rupee lost, and 'miss' does not tell me which is meant.
screens.why3: I know roughly what premium I pay over the bank rate and how the rupee moved, but I never work it out as a percent of my savings for one month, so I would guess, and if I bought no dollars last month the label does not fit.
screens.why4: A percent box works and 'None' fits, but 'I'd rather not say' is a second escape beside 'I can't recall', and the box label about rupees I move to dollars does not match the question's rupees I was saving.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product leaks, but 'value you miss' reads like someone's analysis term rather than my words, and the question has drifted from keeping savings from losing value into an odd measure.
screens.why6: The question can be said in one breath, but 'a percent of the rupees you move to dollars, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful of instructions I would have to hear twice, though the spoken version does keep to one escape.
screens.instead: Last month, about what percent above the bank rate did you pay to turn your rupees into dollars? A box for the percent, with chips: I didn't buy dollars last month; I can't recall.

screens.why1: A fee question makes sense after the Karsa card, but the heading says 'What you do today' and I have told nobody yet how I would use it, so it comes a bit abruptly.
screens.why2: I know percent fees from Binance, but 'a fee on what you move' and then 'a fee a month' do not sit together, so I have to read it twice to work out whether it is per transfer or monthly.
screens.why3: I have paid the dollar premium and Binance costs, so I can say from my own buying what percent would feel fair.
screens.why4: The bands are clear and do not overlap, they run from tiny to more than I would ever pay, and both 'I wouldn't pay a fee' and 'I can't say' fit.
screens.why5: The card shown on purpose is fine, but 'what you move' is the company's way of putting it, since I would say buying or keeping dollars, and 'small' tells me the answer before I give it.
screens.why6: The two steps are easy to hold and the percents say well, but 'a fee on what you move' then 'a fee a month' is confusing when heard once, and 'Or say you can't say' is clumsy.
screens.instead: Karsa takes a small percent of the rupees you change into dollars. What percent would feel fair to you? Under 0.5%; 0.5% to under 1%; 1% to under 2%; 2% to under 5%; 5% or more; I wouldn't pay a fee; or I can't say.

screens.why1: After the fee question it is plausible to ask how the last payment was decided, but it comes abruptly and sits under 'What you do today' when I only heard about Karsa a moment ago.
screens.why2: 'Something like this' makes me read twice, because I am not sure if it means a P2P dollar purchase, a Binance fee, or a service like Karsa, though the rest is simple.
screens.why3: I buy dollars from my own savings and nobody signs off, so I can answer, but I would have to guess what counts as 'like this' since I have never paid for a product like Karsa.
screens.why4: The options cover the cases and the escape fits, but 'No, someone else decided for me' is an odd answer to 'did anyone else have to agree', and the yes and no answers are not in a natural order.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's plan leaks, but 'agree' and 'decided' feel like a company buying process carried over to one person saving their own rupees, so it has drifted a little.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four options and one escape, but the two yes and two no answers are interleaved and sound alike, so they are hard to hold after one hearing, and 'you can't recall one' sounds odd.
screens.instead: The last time you changed rupees into dollars, did anyone else have a say? Options: No, I decided on my own; Yes, a family member had to agree; Yes, someone else decided for me. Escape: I can't recall one.

screens.why1: After the fee and who has to agree, it makes sense to ask whether I would actually put some money in, though the 'What you do today' label above it is off because this is about what I would do.
screens.why2: Buying a small first amount of dollars is how I already think about it, so I get it on first reading.
screens.why3: I have rupees left over and already decide when to turn them into dollars, so I can answer from my own savings.
screens.why4: 'Probably not' sits close to 'No', and there is nothing for someone leaning yes who wants to check it first, but my true answer can still be found here.
screens.why5: The card says dollar stablecoins but the question says just 'dollars', which drifts a little because buying USDT in a wallet is not the same as buying actual dollars.
screens.why6: It is one short question with three options I can hold after hearing it once, and the first option repeating the stem is only slightly long.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you buy a small first amount of dollar stablecoins, or not? Yes, I'd buy a small amount; Probably, after checking it first; Probably not; No.
